# .clavis.yaml

<p class="cli-lead">The per-folder file that links a repository to a project. Commit it; it holds no secrets.</p>

`clavis init` writes `.clavis.yaml` in your repository. Commands look for
it in the current folder and its parents, so they work from any
subfolder without flags.

```yaml
server: https://clavis.example.com
org: acme
project: web-app
env: dev               # default environment
path: /                # default folder
run: bin/rails server  # what a plain `clavis run` starts
branch_envs: true      # use the git branch's preview environment
cache: true            # encrypted offline cache for `clavis run`
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `server` | Server URL. Saved by `clavis login`. |
| `org`, `project` | Organization and project slugs. |
| `env` | Default environment. `--env` overrides it per command. |
| `path` | Default folder inside the environment. |
| `run` | Command started by `clavis run` with no arguments. Quotes and backslashes work as in a shell; pipes and `&&` don't (put those in a script). |
| `branch_envs` | When `true`, use the preview environment of the current git branch if one exists. See [`clavis env branch`](./env-branch). |
| `cache` | When `true`, keep an encrypted copy of the last values for offline use. See [offline cache](./offline-cache). |

## Which value wins

For server, organization, project and environment, the first one set
wins:

1. the flag (`--env staging`)
2. the environment variable (`CLAVIS_ENV=staging`)
3. `.clavis.yaml`
4. the default (`dev` for the environment)

## Examples

<p class="cli-example-title">Save a default command, then start it</p>

```sh
echo 'run: npm run dev' >> .clavis.yaml
clavis run
```
